newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - Paris to decide central bank members Jan 3.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Paris to decide central bank members Jan 3.

text.p: The French government is expected to decide on January 3 on replacements for two members of the Bank of France's monetary policy council (CPM) whose mandate expires in January, CPM member Paul Marchelli said on Thursday.
Marchelli told Reuters that the council, which met earlier on Thursday, had given its opinion on a list of six candidates proposed for the posts.
He declined to say what that opinion was. The CPM gives an opinion on new council members in a purely advisory capacity ahead of a decision by the French cabinet.
The cabinet is next due to meet on January 3.

The make-up of the nine-member monetary council is being closely watched by financial markets for any softening in the independent central bank's tough line on defending the stability of the franc against the mark.
The bank has held French interest rates slightly above German rates in order to protect the franc against any speculative attack on currency markets.

A three-person minority on the council is, however, believed to favour faster rate cuts to boost growth and jobs, taking French rates below German ones if the Bundesbank fails to ease monetary policy further.
Marchelli has argued publicly that French rates could be cut without damaging the franc.
A change in the make-up of the CPM, set up when the central bank became independent in 1994, could tip the balance in favour of that minority.

The mandates of two members of the council, ex-journalist Jean Boissonnat and ex-banker Bruno de Maulde -- given three-year terms when the council first met on January 7, 1994 -- are coming up for renewal.
Both are believed to form part of a six-person majority backing governor Jean-Claude Trichet's very cautious approach to monetary easing. Of the two, only Boissonnat is seeking to stay on.

He is included on a list of six nominees which also includes diplomat Pierre Achard, Alain Prate, former vice-president of the European Investment Bank (EIB), Robert Pelletier, former managing director of the Association of Credit Establishments (Afec), Pierre Guillen, ex-head of the CNPF employers' federation, and Jean-Rene Bernard, formerly head of of regional bank CIC, sources close to the nomination process say.

One source said he believed French President Jacques Chirac had intervened to get Guillen and Bernard on the list of nominees. Both are close to the president and, some say, would favour a faster pace of rate cuts.

Sources close to the nomination process say, however, that Chirac, who earlier this month restated his commitment to a stable franc, was not expected to try to push the bank into any radical departure from that policy.
"You don't change monetary policy the way you change your shirt," Marchelli said.
Chirac's office has declined all comment.
Trichet's own mandate expires at the end of 1999.
